facts.statement: Stegosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian to Tithonian),

facts.statement: The genus Stegosaurus was first described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1877

facts.statement: Stegosaurus remains were first identified by Othniel Charles Marsh during the Bone Wars at Dinosaur Ridge National Landmark.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus remains were first identified during the "Bone Wars" by Othniel Charles Marsh at Dinosaur Ridge National Landmark.

facts.statement: The first Stegosaurus fossils were discovered by Arthur Lakes and H.C. Beckwith north of Morrison, Colorado, at YPM Quarry 5.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus, one of the many dinosaurs described in the Bone Wars, was first discovered by Arthur Lakes and H.C. Beckwith, consisting of several caudal vertebrae, a dermal plate, and several additional postcranial elements that were collected north of Morrison, Colorado, at Lakes' YPM Quarry 5.

facts.statement: The initial fragmented bones found by Lakes and Beckwith became the holotype for Stegosaurus armatus when Marsh described them in 1877.
facts.quote: These first, fragmented bones (YPM 1850) became the holotype of Stegosaurus armatus when Yale paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh described them in 1877.

facts.statement: Marshall P. Felch collected the famous nearly complete Stegosaurus skeleton from his quarry in Garden Park, Colorado, between 1885 and 1886.
facts.quote: Marshall P. Felch collected the skeleton throughout 1885 and 1886 from Morrison Formation strata at his quarry in Garden Park, a town near Cañon City, Colorado.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh named the nearly complete skeleton Stegosaurus stenops in 1887.
facts.quote: The skeleton was shipped to Marsh in 1887, who named it Stegosaurus stenops ( "narrow-faced roof lizard") that year.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus is an extinct herbivorous dinosaur characterized by kite-shaped upright plates on its back and spikes on its tail.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus (; ) is a genus of extinct herbivorous four-legged armored dinosaurs from the Late Jurassic, characterized by the distinctive kite-shaped upright plates along their backs and spikes on their tails.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus were large, heavily built quadrupeds with rounded backs, short forelimbs, long hindlimbs, and tails held high.
facts.quote: They were large, heavily built, herbivorous quadrupeds with rounded backs, short fore limbs, long hind limbs, and tails held high in the air.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had a short neck and small head, suggesting it fed on low-lying bushes and shrubs.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus had a relatively low brain-to-body mass ratio. It had a short neck and a small head, meaning it most likely ate low-lying bushes and shrubs.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus ungulatus is one of the largest stegosaurians, with specimens reaching about 9 meters in length and weighing over 6.9 metric tons.
facts.quote: One species, Stegosaurus ungulatus, is one of the largest known of all the stegosaurians, with the largest known specimens measuring about 9 m long and weighing over 6.9 MT.

facts.statement: Scientists generally agree that Stegosaurus used its spiked tails for defense and its plates primarily for display and secondarily for thermoregulation.
facts.quote: Today, it is generally agreed that their spiked tails were most likely used for defense against predators, while their plates may have been used primarily for display, and secondarily for thermoregulatory functions.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus fossils have been found in the western United States and Portugal, dating from 155 to 145 million years ago.
facts.quote: Fossils of the genus have been found in the western United States and in Portugal, where they are found in Kimmeridgian- to Tithonian-aged strata, dating to between 155 and 145 million years ago.

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Stegosaurus is Stegosaurus stenops.
facts.quote: type_species: Stegosaurus stenops

facts.statement: Hypsirhophus and Diracodon are listed as synonyms of Stegosaurus.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Hypsirhophus? Cope, 1878 Diracodon Marsh, 1881

facts.statement: Marsh originally thought Stegosaurus was an aquatic turtle-like animal and named it based on the idea that its plates overlapped like roof shingles.
facts.quote: Marsh initially believed the remains were from an aquatic turtle-like animal, and the basis for its scientific name, 'roof(ed) lizard' was due to his early belief that the plates lay flat over the animal's back, overlapping like the shingles (tiles) on a roof.

facts.statement: The International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature replaced the original type species with Stegosaurus stenops because the original type specimen was considered dubious.
facts.quote: Because of this, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature decided to replace the type species with the more well known species Stegosaurus stenops.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Hypsirhophus is a synonym of Stegosaurus or a distinct genus based on vertebral differences.
facts.quote: Many later researchers have considered Hypsirhophus to be a synonym of Stegosaurus, though Peter Galton (2010) suggested that it is distinct based on differences in the vertebrae.

facts.statement: A large shoulder spike preserved in Stegosaurus sulcatus is speculated to be a key diagnostic feature for that species.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus sulcatus most notably preserves a large spike that has been speculated to have been a shoulder spike that is used to diagnose the species.

facts.statement: Remains of over 80 individual Stegosaurus animals have been discovered.
facts.quote: The remains of over 80 individual animals of this genus have been found.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus lived alongside Apatosaurus, Diplodocus, Camarasaurus, and Allosaurus, which may have preyed on it.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus would have lived alongside dinosaurs such as Apatosaurus, Diplodocus, Camarasaurus and Allosaurus, the latter of which may have preyed on it.

facts.statement: A skeleton of Stegosaurus stenops has been on display at the National Museum of Natural History in Washington D.C. since 1915.
facts.quote: The skeleton of S. stenops has since been deposited at the National Museum of Natural History in Washington D. C., where it has been on display since 1915.

facts.statement: A composite skeleton of Stegosaurus stenops collected at Quarry 13 in Como Bluff in 1887 was mounted at the National Museum of Natural History, with USNM 6531 being the most complete specimen.
facts.quote: Another mount was made for the NMNH in the form of a mounted composite skeleton consisting of several specimens referred to S. stenops that were collected at Quarry 13 at Como Bluff in 1887, the most complete being USNM 6531.

facts.statement: Richard Swann Lull incorporated the type specimen of Stegosaurus ungulatus into the first mounted stegosaur skeleton at the Peabody Museum of Natural History in 1910.
facts.quote: The type specimen of S. ungulatus (YPM 1853) was incorporated into the first ever mounted skeleton of a stegosaur at the Peabody Museum of Natural History in 1910 by Richard Swann Lull.

facts.statement: Frederick Lucas named the species Stegosaurus marshi in 1901.
facts.quote: The next species of Stegosaurus to be named was S. marshi by Frederick Lucas in 1901.

facts.statement: Until 1918, the only mounted Stegosaurus skeleton in the world was O.C. Marsh's type specimen of S. ungulatus, displayed at the Peabody Museum of Natural History since 1910.
facts.quote: Until 1918, the only mounted skeleton of Stegosaurus in the world was O. C. Marsh's type specimen of S. ungulatus at the Peabody Museum of Natural History, which was put on display in 1910.

facts.statement: The first mounted skeleton depicting Stegosaurus stenops was completed in 1918.
facts.quote: 1918 saw the completion of the second Stegosaurus mount, and the first depicting S. stenops.

facts.statement: Charles Gilmore directed the creation of the first Stegosaurus stenops mount at the U.S. National Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: This mount was created under the direction of Charles Gilmore at the U.S. National Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: A composite mounted skeleton of Stegosaurus stenops was displayed at the American Museum of Natural History in 1932.
facts.quote: A third mounted skeleton of Stegosaurus, referred to S. stenops, was put on display at the American Museum of Natural History in 1932.

facts.statement: A composite mount of Stegosaurus ungulatus made from specimens collected at Dinosaur National Monument between 1920 and 1922 was displayed at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in 1940.
facts.quote: Another composite mount, using specimens referred to S. ungulatus collected from Dinosaur National Monument between 1920 and 1922, was put on display at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in 1940.

facts.statement: The American Museum of Natural History launched an expedition in 1897 that found incomplete Stegosaurus specimens at Bone Cabin Quarry in Como Bluff.
facts.quote: The American Museum of Natural History was the first to launch an expedition in 1897, finding several assorted, but incomplete, Stegosaurus specimens at Bone Cabin Quarry in Como Bluff.

facts.statement: Unpublished Stegosaurus remains from Bone Cabin Quarry were mounted in 1932 as a composite primarily of specimens AMNH 650 and 470.
facts.quote: These remains haven't been described and were mounted in 1932, the mount being a composite primarily of specimens AMNH 650 & 470 from Bone Cabin Quarry.

facts.statement: Carnegie crews discovered dozens of Stegosaurus specimens at Dinosaur National Monument between the 1900s and 1920s.
facts.quote: in the 1900s-1920s Carnegie crews at Dinosaur National Monument discovered dozens of Stegosaurus specimens in one of the greatest single sites for the taxon.

facts.statement: The most complete Stegosaurus skeleton found at Dinosaur National Monument, CM 11341, was used as the basis for a composite mount in 1940.
facts.quote: CM 11341, the most complete skeleton found at the quarry, was used for the basis of a composite Stegosaurus mount in 1940 along with several other specimens to finish the mount.

facts.statement: Carnegie crews found a Stegosaurus cranium, CM 12000, which is one of the few known.
facts.quote: A cranium (CM 12000) was also found by Carnegie crews, one of the few known.

facts.statement: Specimens from the American Museum of Natural History and the Carnegie Museum of Natural History have been referred to Stegosaurus ungulatus.
facts.quote: Both the AMNH and CM material has been referred to Stegosaurus ungulatus.

facts.statement: Four different arrangements for the plates on Stegosaurus have been proposed over the years.
facts.quote: Four possible plate arrangements have been proposed over the years

facts.statement: O.C. Marsh initially interpreted Stegosaurus plates as lying flat like shingles, an idea that led to the nickname 'roof lizard'.
facts.quote: The plates lie flat along the back, as a shingle-like armor. This was Marsh's initial interpretation, which led to the name 'roof lizard'.

facts.statement: Further fossil evidence showed that Stegosaurus plates stood on edge rather than lying flat.
facts.quote: As further and complete plates were found, their form showed they stood on edge, rather than lying flat.

facts.statement: In 1891, O.C. Marsh published an interpretation of Stegosaurus with a single row of plates.
facts.quote: By 1891, Marsh published a more familiar view of Stegosaurus, with a single row of plates.

facts.statement: Stephen Czerkas revived the single-row plate arrangement theory in the 1980s, basing it on the arrangement of iguana dorsal spines.
facts.quote: It was revived, in somewhat modified form, in the 1980s, by Stephen Czerkas, based on the arrangement of iguana dorsal spines.

facts.statement: Charles R. Knight's 1901 reconstruction and the 1933 film King Kong depicted Stegosaurus plates in a double row along the back.
facts.quote: The plates were paired in a double row along the back, such as in Knight's 1901 reconstruction and the 1933 film King Kong.

facts.statement: The theory of alternating rows of plates became the prevalent view by the early 1960s due to partially articulated fossils of S. stenops showing this arrangement.
facts.quote: Two rows of alternating plates. By the early 1960s, this had become (and remains) the prevalent idea, mainly because some S. stenops fossils in which the plates are still partially articulated show this arrangement.

facts.statement: The alternating plate arrangement is chiral, requiring scientists to distinguish specimens from their hypothetical mirror-image forms.
facts.quote: This arrangement is chiral and so demands that a specimen be distinguished from its distinct, hypothetical mirror-image form.

facts.statement: Frederick Lucas later changed his view to believe that Stegosaurus plates were attached in staggered rows.
facts.quote: However, the following year, Lucas wrote that he now believed the plates were probably attached in staggered rows.

facts.statement: Richard Swann Lull suggested in 1910 that the alternating plate pattern in S. stenops was caused by the skeleton shifting after death.
facts.quote: In 1910, Richard Swann Lull wrote that the alternating pattern seen in S. stenops was probably due to shifting of the skeleton after death.

facts.statement: Charles Gilmore argued in 1914 that Stegosaurus plates were preserved in alternating rows near the back peak and showed no evidence of shifting during fossilization.
facts.quote: In 1914, Charles Gilmore argued against Lull's interpretation, noting that several specimens of S. stenops, including the now-completely prepared holotype, preserved the plates in alternating rows near the peak of the back, and that there was no evidence of the plates having shifted relative to the body during fossilization.

facts.statement: The interpretation of paired or staggered rows of plates became the standard, leading to a remount of the Peabody Museum skeleton in 1924.
facts.quote: Gilmore and Lucas' interpretation became the generally accepted standard, and Lull's mount at the Peabody Museum was changed to reflect this in 1924.

facts.statement: Charles J. Long directed a composite Stegosaurus mount at the American Museum of Natural History made of partial remains filled with replicas.
facts.quote: Mounted under the direction of Charles J. Long, the American Museum mount was a composite consisting of partial remains filled in with replicas based on other specimens.

facts.statement: Early Carnegie collections included only a few postcranial remains, but later crews found dozens of specimens at Dinosaur National Monument.
facts.quote: The fossils included only a couple postcranial remains, though in the 1900s-1920s Carnegie crews at Dinosaur National Monument discovered dozens of Stegosaurus specimens in one of the greatest single sites for the taxon.

facts.statement: A significant Stegosaurus fossil was discovered in 1937 at Garden Park by high school teacher Frank Kessler.
facts.quote: An important discovery came in 1937 again at Garden Park by a high school teacher named Frank Kessler

facts.statement: The Stegosaurus skeleton excavated by Robert Landberg was mounted at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science in 1938 by steel worker Phillip Reinheimer.
facts.quote: Phillip Reinheimer, a steel worker, mounted the Stegosaurus skeleton at the DMNS in 1938.

facts.statement: Harold Bollan discovered a 40% complete Stegosaurus skeleton in Rabbit Valley, Colorado, in 1987.
facts.quote: In 1987, a 40% complete Stegosaurus skeleton was discovered in Rabbit Valley in Mesa County, Colorado, by Harold Bollan

facts.statement: The specimen known as Sophie is the best-preserved Stegosaurus, standing 85% intact with 360 bones.
facts.quote: Sophie the Stegosaurus is the best preserved Stegosaurus specimen, being 85% intact and containing 360 bones.

facts.statement: Bob Simon discovered the Sophie Stegosaurus specimen in 2003 at a quarry near Shell, Wyoming.
facts.quote: Sophie was first discovered by Bob Simon in 2003 at a quarry on the Red Canyon Ranch near Shell, Wyoming

facts.statement: A nearly complete Stegosaurus skeleton nicknamed Apex sold for $44.6 million at a Sotheby's auction in New York City on July 17, 2024.
facts.quote: On July 17, 2024, a nearly complete, 27-foot (8.2m) long Stegosaurus skeleton, nicknamed "Apex", fetched $44.6m (£34m) at a Sotheby's auction in New York City

facts.statement: Stegosaurus is a quadrupedal dinosaur easily recognized by a double row of vertical kite-shaped plates on its back and two pairs of horizontal spikes at the tail's end.
facts.quote: The quadrupedal Stegosaurus is one of the most easily identifiable dinosaur genera, due to the distinctive double row of kite-shaped plates rising vertically along the rounded back and the two pairs of long spikes extending horizontally near the end of the tail.

facts.statement: S. stenops measured 6.5 meters in length and 3.5 metric tons in mass, while S. ungulatus reached 7 meters in length and 3.8 metric tons in mass.
facts.quote: S. stenops reached 6.5 m in length and 3.5 MT in body mass, while S. ungulatus reached 7 m in length and 3.8 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: Some large Stegosaurus individuals may have reached lengths of 7.5 to 9 meters and masses of 5.0 to 5.3 metric tons.
facts.quote: Some large individuals may have reached 7.5-9 m in length and 5.0 - 5.3 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: A subadult Stegosaurus discovered in Wyoming in 1994 was 4.6 meters long, 2 meters high, and estimated to weigh between 1.5 and 2.2 metric tons.
facts.quote: One subadult specimen, discovered in 1994 in Wyoming, is 4.6 m long and 2 m high, and is estimated to have weighed 1.5-2.2 metric tons (1.6-2.4 short tons) while alive.

facts.statement: A Stegosaurus skeleton remained on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science until 1989, when an expedition was sent to find additional remains for a hall revision.
facts.quote: The skeleton remained mounted until 1989 when the museum curator of the DMNS began a revision of the museum's fossil hall and dispatched an expedition to find additional Stegosaurus remains.

facts.statement: In 2007, researchers described a Stegosaurus specimen from Portugal originally attributed to the Alcobaça Formation but later suggested to belong to the Lourinhã Formation.
facts.quote: In 2007, Escaso and colleagues described a Stegosaurus specimen from the Casal Novo locality of Portugal, originally thought to be part of the Alcobaça Formation, and subsequently suggested to be part of the Lourinhã Formation.

facts.statement: The Apex Stegosaurus skeleton was discovered in 2022 on private land in Colorado, allowing it to be sold to a private owner.
facts.quote: The specimen had been discovered in 2022 on private land in Colorado and so could be sold to a private owner.

facts.statement: While the owner of the Apex skeleton allows scientific research, private ownership of such fossils remains controversial among researchers who argue for permanent institutional curation.
facts.quote: The current owner has made "Apex" available for scientific research, but private ownership of important fossil specimens is controversial, with many researchers insisting that fossils be permanently curated at a formal institution for universal scientific access.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had a long, narrow skull that was small relative to its body size.
facts.quote: The long and narrow skull was small in proportion to the body.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the low position of the skull indicates Stegosaurus likely browsed low-growing vegetation.
facts.quote: The skull's low position suggests that Stegosaurus may have been a browser of low-growing vegetation.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus possessed small, triangular, flat teeth with wear facets indicating they ground their food.
facts.quote: Stegosaurian teeth were small, triangular, and flat; wear facets show that they did grind their food.

facts.statement: Despite its large body size, the braincase of Stegosaurus was small, no larger than that of a dog.
facts.quote: Despite the animal's overall size, the braincase of Stegosaurus was small, being no larger than that of a dog.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus stenops has 27 vertebrae before the sacrum, four sacral vertebrae in most subadults, and around 46 tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: In Stegosaurus stenops there are 27 bones in the vertebral column anterior to the sacrum, a varying number of vertebrae in the sacrum, with four in most subadults, and around 46 caudal (tail) vertebrae.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had three short toes on each hind foot and five toes on each fore foot, with only the inner two fore toes bearing blunt hooves.
facts.quote: The hind feet each had three short toes, while each fore foot had five toes; only the inner two toes had a blunt hoof.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus had much shorter forelimbs than its stocky hind limbs, resulting in an unusual posture.
facts.quote: The fore limbs were much shorter than the stocky hind limbs, which resulted in an unusual posture.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus likely held its tail off the ground while keeping its head low, no higher than 1 meter above the ground.
facts.quote: The tail appears to have been held well clear of the ground, while the head of Stegosaurus was positioned relatively low down, probably no higher than 1 m above the ground.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus plates were not directly attached to the skeleton but arose from the skin.
facts.quote: They were not directly attached to the animal's skeleton, instead arising from the skin.

facts.statement: Evidence from Hesperosaurus suggests Stegosaurus plates were covered in keratinous sheaths, indicated by smooth surfaces with long, parallel, shallow grooves.
facts.quote: Well preserved integumentary impressions of the plates of Hesperosaurus show a smooth surface with long and parallel, shallow grooves. This indicates that the plates were covered in keratinous sheaths.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus often falls within the subclade Stegosaurinae, which typically includes Wuerhosaurus and Hesperosaurus.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus frequently is discovered in a clade within the Stegosauridae called Stegosaurinae, usually including the taxa Wuerhosaurus and Hesperosaurus.

facts.statement: A 2019 study suggests that the sister group to Stegosauria, Ankylosauria, may have originated in the early Early Jurassic based on fossil evidence from India.
facts.quote: Galton (2019) interpreted plates of an armored dinosaur from the Lower Jurassic (Sinemurian-Pliensbachian) Lower Kota Formation of India as fossils of a member of Ankylosauria; the author argued that this finding indicates a probable early Early Jurassic origin for both Ankylosauria and its sister group Stegosauria.

facts.statement: The species Stegosaurus stenops was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1887, with its holotype collected by Marshall Felch in Colorado in 1886.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus stenops, meaning "narrow-faced roof lizard", was named by Marsh in 1887, with the holotype having been collected by Marshall Felch at Garden Park, north of Cañon City, Colorado, in 1886.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus stenops possessed proportionately large, broad plates along its back and rounded plates on its tail.
facts.quote: It had proportionately large, broad plates and rounded tail plates.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence shows that the plates on Stegosaurus stenops were arranged in an alternating, staggered double row.
facts.quote: Articulated specimens show that the plates were arranged alternating in a staggered double row.

facts.statement: Over 50 partial skeletons, one complete skull, and four partial skulls of Stegosaurus stenops have been found.
facts.quote: S. stenops is known from at least 50 partial skeletons of adults and juveniles, one complete skull, and four partial skulls.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus stenops was shorter than other species in the genus, reaching a length of 6.5 meters.
facts.quote: It was shorter than other species, at 6.5 m.

facts.statement: Confirmed remains of Stegosaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation's stratigraphic zones 2 through 6, with possible remains from zone 1.
facts.quote: Confirmed Stegosaurus remains have been found in the Morrison Formation's stratigraphic zones 2–6, with additional remains possibly referrable to Stegosaurus recovered from stratigraphic zone 1.

facts.statement: The species Stegosaurus ungulatus was named by Marsh in 1879 from remains found at Como Bluff, Wyoming.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus ungulatus, meaning "hoofed roof lizard", was named by Marsh in 1879, from remains recovered at Como Bluff, Wyoming (Quarry 12, near Robber's Roost).

facts.statement: Stegosaurus ungulatus was the largest species in the genus, measuring between 7 and 9 meters in length and weighing approximately 6.9 tonnes.
facts.quote: At 7-9 m in length and 6.9 tonnes (7.6 short tons) in weight, it was the largest species within the genus Stegosaurus.

facts.statement: The small, flat, spine-like plates found just before the tail spikes on Stegosaurus ungulatus appear to have been paired.
facts.quote: These spine-like plates appear to have been paired, due to the presence of at least one pair that are identical but mirrored.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Stegosaurus ungulatus was discovered with eight tail spikes, although they were found scattered away from their original positions.
facts.quote: The type specimen of S. ungulatus was discovered with eight spikes, though they were scattered away from their original positions.

facts.statement: Specimens referred to Stegosaurus ungulatus from other quarries, such as those forming part of the AMNH 650 composite skeleton, are preserved with only four tail spikes.
facts.quote: Specimens from other quarries (such as a tail from Quarry 13, now forming part of the composite skeleton AMNH 650 at the American Museum of Natural History), referred to S. ungulatus on the basis of their notched tail vertebrae, are preserved with only four tail spikes.

facts.statement: The first mounted skeleton of Stegosaurus ungulatus was initially displayed with plates set wide above the ribs, but was remounted in 1924 with plates in two staggered rows along the midline of the back.
facts.quote: It was initially mounted with paired plates set wide, above the base of the ribs, but was remounted in 1924 with two staggered rows of plates along the midline of the back.

facts.statement: Richard Swann Lull incorporated the type specimen of Stegosaurus ungulatus into the first ever mounted stegosaur skeleton at the Peabody Museum of Natural History in 1910.
facts.quote: The type specimen of S. ungulatus (YPM 1853) was incorporated into the first ever mounted skeleton of a stegosaur at the Peabody Museum of Natural History in 1910 by Richard Swann Lull.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus sulcatus was described by Marsh in 1887 based on a partial skeleton.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus sulcatus, meaning "furrowed roof lizard", was described by Marsh in 1887 based on a partial skeleton.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that a large spike associated with the type specimen of S. sulcatus may originate from the shoulder or hip rather than the tail, due to its unusually large base.
facts.quote: A spike associated with the type specimen, originally thought to be a tail spike, may in fact come from the shoulder or hip, since its base is much larger than the corresponding tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: A 2008 review by Maidment and colleagues suggested that Stegosaurus sulcatus might be an indeterminate species belonging to a different genus rather than Stegosaurus.
facts.quote: A review published by Maidment and colleagues in 2008 regarded it as an indeterminate species possibly not even belonging to Stegosaurus at all, but to a different genus.

facts.statement: In 2008, Susannah Maidment and colleagues proposed a taxonomy where S. stenops and S. ungulatus were synonymized with S. armatus, and Hesperosaurus and Wuerhosaurus were sunk into Stegosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2008, Susannah Maidment and colleagues proposed extensive alterations to the taxonomy of Stegosaurus. They advocated synonymizing S. stenops and S. ungulatus with S. armatus, and sinking Hesperosaurus and Wuerhosaurus into Stegosaurus, with their type species becoming Stegosaurus mjosi and Stegosaurus homheni, respectively.

facts.statement: In 2015, Maidment and colleagues revised their taxonomy after Galton recognized S. armatus as a nomen dubium and replaced it with S. stenops as the type species.
facts.quote: In 2015, Maidment et al. revised their suggestion due to the recognition by Galton of S. armatus as a nomen dubium and its replacement by S. stenops as type species.

facts.statement: The original type specimen of Stegosaurus armatus was very fragmentary, containing only a partial tail, hips, legs, some back vertebrae, and a single plate.
facts.quote: However, the type specimen was very fragmentary, consisting only of a partial tail, hips, and leg, parts of some back vertebrae, and a single fragmentary plate

facts.statement: Due to the extreme fragmentary nature of the type specimen, Stegosaurus armatus is now generally considered a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: Because the type specimen is very fragmentary, it is extremely difficult to compare it with other species based on better specimens, and it is now generally considered to be a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus affinis, named by Marsh in 1881, is known only from a pubis bone that has since been lost.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus "affinis", named by Marsh in 1881, is only known from a pubis which has since been lost.

facts.statement: Diracodon laticeps was described by Marsh in 1881 based on jawbone fragments.
facts.quote: Diracodon laticeps was described by Marsh in 1881, from some jawbone fragments.

facts.statement: Bakker resurrected Diracodon laticeps in 1986 as a senior synonym of S. stenops, though others argue the material is non-diagnostic and represents a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: Bakker resurrected D. laticeps in 1986 as a senior synonym of S. stenops, although others note that the material is not diagnostic and is only referable to Stegosaurus sp., making it a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus duplex, meaning "two plexus roof lizard" due to an enlarged sacral neural canal, was named by Marsh in 1887.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus duplex, meaning "two plexus roof lizard" (in allusion to the greatly enlarged neural canal of the sacrum which Marsh characterized as a "posterior brain case"), was named by Marsh in 1887 (including the holotype specimen).

facts.statement: The disarticulated bones of Stegosaurus duplex were collected in 1879 by Edward Ashley at Como Bluff.
facts.quote: The disarticulated bones were actually collected in 1879 by Edward Ashley at Como Bluff.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus marshi, described by Lucas in 1901, was renamed Hoplitosaurus in 1902.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus marshi, which was described by Lucas in 1901, was renamed Hoplitosaurus in 1902.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus priscus, described by Nopcsa in 1911, was reassigned to Lexovisaurus and is now the type species of Loricatosaurus.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus priscus, described by Nopcsa in 1911, was reassigned to Lexovisaurus, and is now the type species of Loricatosaurus.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus madagascariensis from Madagascar is known only from teeth and was described by Piveteau in 1926.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus madagascariensis from Madagascar is known solely from teeth and was described by Piveteau in 1926.

facts.statement: The teeth of Stegosaurus madagascariensis were variously attributed to a stegosaur, Majungasaurus, a hadrosaur, or a crocodylian, but are now considered to belong to a possible ankylosaur.
facts.quote: The teeth were variously attributed to a stegosaur, the theropod Majungasaurus, a hadrosaur or even a crocodylian, but is now considered a possible ankylosaur.

facts.statement: Stegosaurus homheni is an alternative name for the Chinese Cretaceous stegosaur Wuerhosaurus homheni, described in 1973 by Dong Zhiming.
facts.quote: Stegosaurus homheni is an alternative combination for the Chinese Cretaceous stegosaur Wuerhosaurus homheni, which was described based on a partial postcranial skeleton in 1973 by Dong Zhiming.

facts.statement: Although referred to Stegosaurus in 2008 by Maidment et al., Wuerhosaurus homheni is generally regarded as belonging to its own genus.
facts.quote: It was referred to Stegosaurus in 2008 by Maidment et al., but the species is generally regarded to be in its own genus.

facts.statement: The hypothesis that Stegosaurus could rear up on its hind legs was proposed by Bakker and opposed by Carpenter.
facts.quote: This has been proposed by Bakker and opposed by Carpenter.
